title: How to install Tailwind CSS with Nuxt.js and Flowbite

segments.text: [Nuxt.js](https://nuxtjs.org/) is a free and open-source JavaScript framework based on Vue.js that helps you develop modern web applications using SSR (server-side rendering) which provides a faster load, better SEO (search engine optimization), and better caching capabilities.
The framework was inspired by Vercel's Next.js framework built with React and it is being used by large companies such as Ecosia, Upwork, NASA, Appsumo, and CDN JS.
If you follow this guide you will learn how to install the latest version 3 of Nuxt.js with Tailwind CSS and Flowbite and also show you how to use the TypeScript version.

segments.text: Before continuing make sure that you have Node.js and NPM installed on your local machine.

segments.heading: Create a Nuxt.js project

```bash

```

segments.text: Install the project dependencies by executing the following command:

segments.text: Run the following command to start a local development server on `http://localhost:3000/`:

title: How to set up Ruby on Rails with Tailwind CSS and Flowbite

segments.text: _Disclaimer: this guide has been first published on the Flowbite integration docs for [Tailwind CSS and Ruby on Rails](https://flowbite.com/docs/getting-started/rails/)._

[Ruby on Rails](https://rubyonrails.org/) is an open-source full-stack web application framework that runs server-side written in Ruby and built by the creators of Basecamp based on a model-view-controller architecture.
Popular websites such as GitHub, Shopify, Twitch, Dribbble, AirBnB, Coinbase are all based on the Ruby on Rails framework and it is continued to be used by thousands of companies and developers.

In this guide you will learn how to set up Ruby on Rails with [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com) and install [Flowbite](https://flowbite.com) to start using the UI components built with the utility classes from Tailwind CSS.

title: How to install Symfony with Flowbite and Tailwind CSS

segments.text: [Symfony](https://symfony.com/) is one of the definitive web application frameworks in the PHP ecosystem offering over 50 standalone PHP components and a MVC framework for your web application that you can use to build complex applications, website pages and even API services.

The Symfony PHP framework was first launched as an open-source software back in 2005 by SensioLabs SAS and it is currently used by numerous companies and frameworks including Laravel, Spotify, BlaBlaCar, Trivago, Dailymotion and more.

Follow the steps from this guide to learn how to create a new Symfony project on your local computer, install and configure the Tailwind CSS framework, and finally install Flowbite and leverage the open-source UI components to build websites even faster.

segments.heading: Requirements
segments.text: Make sure that before you get started you have both [PHP](https://www.php.net/) (v8.1 or higher), [Composer](https://getcomposer.org/download/) and [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/) installed on your local environment so that Symfony, Tailwind CSS and Flowbite can be properly set up and configured.

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: The most straightforward approach for creating a new Symfony project is to use the official [Symfony CLI](https://symfony.com/download) installer which you can easily install on macOS and Linux devices using Homebrew:

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text:
```bash
brew install symfony-cli/tap/symfony-cli
```

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: For devices running on Windows you can also install the Symfony CLI using Scoop:

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text:
```bash
scoop install symfony-cli
```

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: Now that you have the CLI available you can proceed by creating a new project.

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: Create a new Symfony project by running the following command inside your terminal:

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text:
```bash
symfony new --webapp my_application
```

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: This command will create a new folder with a fresh Symfony project installation inside.

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: Install the recommended Symfony Webpack Encore bundle to enable front-end integration via Composer:

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text:
```bash
composer require symfony/webpack-encore-bundle
```

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: Run the following command in your terminal to start a local web server:

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text:
```bash
symfony server:start
```

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: This command will make the web application accessible via the browser on `http://localhost:8000`.

segments.heading: Create a Symfony project
segments.text: To deploy your application on a server we recommend you to check out the official [production deployment tools and bundlers](https://symfony.com/doc/current/deployment.html) that Symfony provides out-of-the-box, such as Deployer, Ansistrano, or Fabric.

segments.heading: Making the elements interactive
segments.text: In order to make the elements such as the navbar, sidebar and the dropdowns interactive you will have to [install Flowbite](https://flowbite.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/) in your project.

segments.heading: Getting started
segments.text: Flowbite can be included as a plugin into an existing Tailwind CSS project and it is supposed to help you build websites faster by having a set of web components to work with built with the utility classes from Tailwind CSS.

segments.heading: Install using NPM
segments.text: Make sure that you have Node.js and Tailwind CSS installed.

segments.heading: Install using NPM
segments.text: Install Flowbite as a dependency using NPM by running the following command:

segments.text:


segments.text: Require Flowbite as a plugin inside the `tailwind.config.js` file:

Install using NPM

segments.heading: Include via CDN
segments.text: The quickest way to get started working with Flowbite is to simply include the CSS and JavaScript into your project via a CDN service such as UNPKG or CDNJS (content delivery networks).

segments.text: Our component is almost complete, but we need to make some final adjustments to ensure it’s fully accessible and prevent any content from flickering on page load.

segments.heading: Improving Accessibility
segments.text: To make our modal fully accessible, we assign the `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, and an `id` that corresponds to the `aria-controls` attribute assigned to the button element. This indicates that the button is capable of controlling the dialog.

segments.heading: Improving Accessibility
segments.text: Since the button doesn’t have any text to describe its content, we add the `aria-label="Watch the video"` attribute.

segments.heading: Improving Accessibility
segments.text: We also want to remove the button’s outline on click while maintaining accessibility requirements. For this, we add some Tailwind CSS classes that remove the outline on click (`focus:outline-none`) and enable focus for keyboard users (`focus-visible:ring` `focus-visible:ring-indigo-300`).

segments.heading: Improving Accessibility
segments.text: Additionally, we assign the `aria-hidden="true"` attribute to the backdrop to indicate that it’s purely decorative.

segments.heading: Preventing hidden content from flickering on page load
segments.text: By default, the modal is hidden on page load, but there’s a moment during navigation when Alpine.js isn’t fully loaded on the page. As a result, any elements that are supposed to be hidden will flicker on page load.

segments.heading: Preventing hidden content from flickering on page load
segments.text: To avoid this, we can use the `x-cloak` directive to hide the elements that should be hidden by default (in our case, the backdrop and the modal), and add the Tailwind CSS class `[&_[x-cloak]]:hidden` that sets a `display: none` rule to a parent tag.

title: Learn how to install Qwik with Tailwind CSS and Flowbite

segments.text: In this tutorial I want to show you how to create a new Qwik project, configure Tailwind CSS and install the UI component library called Flowbite so you can use a modern and instant-loading front-end stack to build web apps.

segments.heading: Introducing Qwik
segments.text: [Qwik](https://qwik.builder.io/) is a free and open-source front-end framework built by the team behind Builder that allows you to build instant-loading, scalable and interactive web apps by leveraging the precision lazy-loading feature by asynchronously loading component rendering, tasks, listeners, and styles.

segments.heading: Introducing Qwik
segments.text: The framework was first released on July 18th, 2021 by Adam Bradley and Miško Hevery and has a large community of active developers with a popular GitHub repository with over 18k stars and has a showcase of websites such as Builder.io, Reflact.app, Soundy.cloud and more that rely on Qwik for building websites.

segments.heading: Introducing Qwik
segments.text: By following this guide you will learn how to create a new Qwik project, install and configure Tailwind CSS and proceed by installing Flowbite to start leveraging the open-source UI components to build interactive and instant-loading websites faster.

segments.heading: Requirements
segments.text: Before getting started make sure that you have [Node.js v16.8](https://nodejs.org/en) or higher available on your local machine and we also recommend to install the [Qwik VS Code Extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=johnreemar.vscode-qwik-snippets) to enable Qwik snippets.

segments.heading: Create a Qwik project
segments.text: Create a new project by running the following command in your terminal:

segments.heading: Create a Qwik project
segments.text:
```bash
npm create qwik@latest
```

segments.heading: Create a Qwik project
segments.text: The custom CLI (command line interface) from Qwik will prompt you with some questions on how you want your project to be configured - follow the steps until you have a fully working directory.

segments.heading: Create a Qwik project
segments.text: Start a local development server by running:

segments.heading: Create a Qwik project
segments.text:
```bash
npm run start
```

segments.heading: Create a Qwik project
segments.text: You should now be able to access a boilerplate Qwik project on `http://localhost:5173/` from your local browser and start developing with the framework.

segments.heading: Install Tailwind CSS
segments.text: [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/) is a popular utility-first CSS framework that allows you to quickly build website user interfaces by directly writing the CSS and styles in your HTML templates via the rich collection of utility classes.

segments.heading: Install Tailwind CSS
segments.text: The easiest way to set up Tailwind CSS within your Qwik project is to run a starter script command:

segments.heading: Install Tailwind CSS
segments.text:
```bash
npm run qwik add tailwind
```

segments.heading: Install Tailwind CSS
segments.text: This command will automatically set up the following:

segments.heading: Install Tailwind CSS
segments.text:
- install Tailwind CSS and its dependencies
- create a boilerplate `tailwind.config.js` and `postcss.config.js` file
- modify the `src/global.css` file to import the Tailwind modules

segments.heading: Install Tailwind CSS
segments.text: By restarting the sever you will now be able to use the utility-first classes from Tailwind CSS.

segments.heading: Install Flowbite
segments.text: [Flowbite](https://flowbite.com) is a popular open-source UI component library that is built on top of the Tailwind CSS framework leveraging the utility-first class approach with custom interactive JavaScript that allows you to use and customize a collection of components like dropdowns, navbars, modals, and more.

segments.heading: Install Flowbite
segments.text: Follow the next steps to install and set up Flowbite in your Qwik project:

segments.heading: Install Flowbite
segments.text: Install Flowbite via NPM inside your terminal:

segments.heading: Install Flowbite
segments.text:
```bash
npm install flowbite
```

segments.heading: Install Flowbite
segments.text: Require the Flowbite Plugin inside your `tailwind.config.js` configuration file:

segments.heading: Install Flowbite
Install Flowbite
segments.text: Set up the template paths for the dynamic classes file inside the configuration file:

segments.heading: Install Flowbite
Install Flowbite
segments.text: Finally, in the `src/root.tsx` file import the Flowbite JavaScript file inside your Qwik project to start using interactive components that require JavaScript such as the navbars, dropdowns, drawers, and more:

segments.heading: Install Flowbite
Install Flowbite
segments.text: Congratulations! Now you can start using all of the UI components from the Flowbite Library inside your Qwik project together with Tailwind CSS and build websites and user interfaces even faster.

title: Learn how to install Blazor (.NET) with Flowbite and Tailwind CSS

segments.text: [Blazor](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/apps/aspnet/web-apps/blazor) is an open source .NET framework for building dynamic and interactive frontends for your applications with HTML, C#, and Razor templates. Blazor allows you to compose components directly for your server or for the client-side. This flexibility enables developers to create fullstack web and mobile applications with a single-page UI framework.

Typically, most frontend frameworks use JavaScript under the hood but with Blazor, you can build both frontends and backends with C#. Developers who are well versed in C# can easily build fullstack applications without switching to a different framework.

More companies are adopting Blazor into their development workflows because a developer can write client-side and server-side logic with only C# and .NET. Some examples include  GE Aviation, BurnRate, The Postage, and Pernod Ricard.
Blazor provides all the scaffolding, abstractions, tooling and optimizations you need on a project.
[Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com) is a popular and open-source utility first CSS framework that has grown in adoption the past few years with the rise of UI libraries.

[Flowbite](https://flowbite.com) is another popular and open-source UI component library that is based on Tailwind CSS and can help you build websites even faster where you can leverage elements like dropdowns, modals, navbars, and more.

segments.text: In this guide you will learn how to build a new Blazor Project, and how to integrate Flowbite UI components into your application. We'll use a modal component for this exercise to demonstrate a real use case.

segments.heading: **1. What is Material Tailwind? What are its Advantages?**
segments.text: **[Material Tailwind](https://material-tailwind.com/)** is a component library, in other words - an innovative “extension” - of the popular utility-first CSS framework, Tailwind CSS. It offers developers a collection of ready-made components that adhere to modern web design standards. Unlike basic Tailwind CSS, which focuses on utility classes for crafting designs, Material Tailwind provides a suite of pre-styled components, such as[ navigation bars](https://www.material-tailwind.com/docs/html/navbar),[ buttons](https://www.material-tailwind.com/docs/html/button), and[ cards](https://www.material-tailwind.com/docs/html/card). This means less time designing from scratch and more time refining and customizing.

segments.heading: **1. What is Material Tailwind? What are its Advantages?**
segments.text: **Why use Material Tailwind:**

segments.heading: **1. What is Material Tailwind? What are its Advantages?**
segments.text:
* Rapid Development: With a variety of components at your fingertips, creating web pages becomes faster.
* Consistent and Modern Aesthetics: Material Tailwind ensures that all components have a unified, beautiful look. This consistent design language enhances user experience and lends a professional touch to websites.
* Customizable Design: While Material Tailwind provides default styles, the underlying power of Tailwind CSS means every component is highly customizable. Want a button with a different shade or a card with a unique layout? The flexibility is all yours.
* Mobile-Responsive: Material Tailwind components are designed with responsiveness in mind, ensuring they look and function well on screens of all sizes.
* Active Community and Regular Updates: Backed by a community of enthusiastic developers,[ Material Tailwind](https://github.com/creativetimofficial/material-tailwind) benefits from regular updates, new component additions, and community-driven enhancements.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Welcome to a simple guide on building a **CRUD** (Create, Read, Update, Delete) **Task Manager** app using Angular! In this blog, we’ll walk you through creating a functional task management application that allows users to *add*, *view*, *complete*, and *delete* tasks. Whether you’re new to Angular or just looking to reinforce your skills, this tutorial will help you understand the basics of Angular, Tailwind CSS, and how they work together to create a sleek and efficient task manager.

segments.text: Before we dive into the development process, feel free to check out the live view of the task manager app we’ll be building. [Here’s the link to the live view](https://tasks.ayushdev.com/), where you can interact with the app and get a feel for its functionalities.

segments.text: Before we get started, make sure you have the following installed on your machine:

segments.heading: Completing Tasks: Marking Tasks as Completed
segments.text: This section will implement the functionality to mark tasks as completed in the Task List component. We’ll introduce a new `Task` interface to represent each task with a `name` and `completed` property. The `completed` property will track whether a task is marked as completed or not.

segments.heading: Removing Tasks: Deleting Tasks from the List
segments.text: That’s it. this, your super simple task manager application is complete now. Let’s see some possible ideas for enhancements to this application.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: While you’ve successfully created a basic task manager app, there’s always room for improvement and additional features. Here are some ideas for future enhancements to make your app even more useful and user-friendly:

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 1. **Task Categories and Filtering:** Allow users to categorize tasks and provide filtering options to view tasks based on their categories. This can help users organize and manage their tasks more effectively.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 2. **Task Prioritization:** Add the ability to set task priorities, such as high, medium, and low. Users can then sort tasks based on their priority levels.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 3. **Task Due Dates and Reminders:** Enable users to set due dates for tasks and receive reminders or notifications to complete tasks on time.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 4. **Task Notes and Attachments:** Allow users to add notes or attach files to tasks, providing additional context or resources related to each task.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 5. **User Accounts and Data Persistence:** Implement user authentication and data persistence, so users can save their tasks across sessions and access them securely.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 6. **Drag and Drop Reordering:** Implement a drag-and-drop feature to reorder tasks in the list, giving users greater control over the arrangement of tasks.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 7. **Task Sharing and Collaboration:** Introduce task-sharing capabilities, allowing users to collaborate on tasks with others and assign tasks to team members.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 8. **Dark Mode:** Offer a dark mode option to enhance user experience and reduce eye strain, especially during late-night usage.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 9. **Task Analytics and Insights:** Provide users with visual analytics and insights on task completion rates, trends, and productivity statistics.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: 10. **Mobile App Version:** Develop a mobile app version of your task manager to extend its usability and reach to mobile device users.

segments.heading: Future Enhancements: Taking Your Task Manager App to the Next Level
segments.text: Continuous improvement and innovation will keep your task manager app relevant and valuable to users.

title: How to Install and Set Up Tailwind CSS from Scratch

segments.text: **Tailwind CSS** is a popular CSS framework that enables developers to style within their HTML. It simplifies styling through pre-defined classes. If you want to build a personal portfolio website to share your skills and projects, this tutorial will guide you to quickly set up and configure Tailwind CSS.

title: How to Install Radix UI: A Step-by-Step Guide

segments.text: Ever found yourself needing some snazzy, accessible UI components but didn't want to spend hours coding them from scratch? Radix UI has got your back!
